catalog_quote: Finally, it is also relevant to note that Lutuv syllables are limited to three types: open syllables (CV), closed syllables ending in a velar nasal (CVN), which can both be collectively referred to as major syllables, and minor syllables (Cə) which occur as part of an iambic “sesquisyllabic” structure (CəCV). Matisoff (1973:86) coined the term sesquisyllabic to describe these “syllable and a half” structures, which are common in many Tibeto-Burman languages. The first syllable in these sesquisyllabic structures is very short. In Lutuv, the nucleus of a minor syllable is always /ə/, but all vowels can appear as the nucleus of an open syllable. ... As Lutuv is a tonal language, pitch patterns are indicated where possible. ... As our analysis of tone in Lutuv is in its infancy, readers can consider the below marking to be an indication of surface pitch. Three surface pitches are marked: high (á), low (à), and mid (ā). Combined with the moraic representations above, these can be used to represent a fall or rise across a syllable, such as in the second syllable of suohning [sūōn̥ɪ́ŋ̀], ‘two’.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Lutuv is a tone language (three surface pitches H/M/L, analysis preliminary). Words are monosyllabic major syllables (CV or CVŋ, bimoraic) or sesquisyllables Cə.CV(ŋ) in which the initial minor syllable (monomoraic, always /ə/, 'very short') is the weak member of an iambic pattern, i.e. prominence falls on the final major syllable. No independent word-stress contrast is described; nothing beyond this iambic sesquisyllable remark is said about stress.
new_statements.exceptions: None stated. Table 2 marks surface pitch (H/L/M, plus rise/fall on bimoraic rhymes) on sample words; pitch of minor syllables is marked mid (e.g. pakaa [pə̄káá] 'plate').
new_statements.domain_note: Word level, elicited citation forms from one native speaker (co-author Sui Hnem Par, Hnaring village); the authors state their tone analysis is 'in its infancy' and give no statement on word stress as such; the only prominence claim is the 'iambic' characterisation of Cə.CV sesquisyllables (minor syllable short and weak, major syllable strong).
new_statements.first_reading: tone language with a stress statement
new_statements.identity_note: All first-hand sources describe Hnaring Lutuv, the variety of Hnaring village (southern Lutuv area, Thantlang Township, Chin State), from a single consultant (Sui Hnem Par); Glottolog laut1236 lists no dialect nodes. 'Lutuv' is the community's own name; Glottolog/ISO use 'Lautu'. Lutuv/Lautu (Maraic, South Central/Kuki-Chin) is distinct from Mara [mrh], Zophei [zyp] and Senthang [sez].

new_statements.quote: [fn. 12, p. 40] "The Lutuv tone system is in need of more research, but preliminary fieldwork suggests the use of three pitch levels is also warranted." [p. 44] "In Tibeto-Burman languages more broadly, syllable shape descriptions often divide syllables first into minor and major syllables. This split describes the difference between the first and second syllables of an iamb, as in the Zophei word pa hnaa 'snore'. Matisoff (1989) refers to this minor+major syllable iambic structure as a 'sesquisyllable'. More than one minor syllable may precede a major syllable, but minor syllables are never found on the final edge of a prosodic word or phrase." [p. 49] "Since structure of the 'sesquisyllable' in SC languages favors iambic feet, prosodically weak-strong, over trochaic feet, prosodically strong-weak, it is not often clear whether contouring is licensed by the final edge or the prominent syllable."

new_statements.relation_note: Compatible with the existing statement from Bohnert, Berkson & Par 2022 (Lutuv is tonal; minor Cə + major syllable form an iambic sesquisyllabic structure) and with the catalog's empty rule. It adds the family-level framing (minor syllables never word-final, SC favors iambic weak-strong feet, prominence on the final major syllable) and confirms Lutuv is tonal with three pitch levels, but gives no Lutuv-specific word-stress statement, so it does not fill the catalog rule.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Family-level survey of tone in South Central (Kuki-Chin) languages. It does not state a word-stress rule for Lutuv or for any SC language; the only Lutuv-specific content is a footnote saying the Lutuv tone system needs more research and preliminary fieldwork supports three pitch levels. At the family level it describes words as sesquisyllables (one or more reduced 'minor' syllables before a full 'major' syllable), treats the minor+major sequence as an iamb, says minor syllables never end a prosodic word or phrase, and says SC favors iambic weak-strong feet, so the prominent syllable is the final major syllable. The word 'stress' appears only about Stilson 1866 on Kemi/Mro-Khimi (p. 36), in the general 'attractors' discussion (p. 49), and in a fieldwork checklist (p. 60).
new_statements.exceptions: None for Lutuv. The paper notes minor-syllable tone behaves differently across SC languages (toneless in Hakha Lai and Lemi, contrastive in Zophei, sec. 5.1 p. 45), and that the language is tonal (three pitch levels for Lutuv per fn. 12).
new_statements.identity_note: Lotven 2023 is a South Central (Kuki-Chin) family survey adapted from Lotven 2021 on Lawngtlang Zophei; its examples are Zophei, Hakha Lai, Falam, Kuki-Thaadow, Senthang, Mara etc. Lutuv (the catalog's Hnaring Lutuv, ISO clt) is named once, in fn. 12 p. 40, as a Maraic language whose tone system needs more research. The iambic-sesquisyllable statements are made for SC languages generally, not for Lutuv specifically.
